title: How much does a website cost in Delhi in 2026?
author: ER Freelancer
excerpt: Typical 2026 price ranges for business websites, online stores and web apps in Delhi NCR, what actually changes the quote, and the running costs most people forget.
content:
Ask five developers in Delhi what a website costs and you will hear five very different numbers. The gap is rarely about the developer's rate alone. It comes from what is being built, how much of it is custom, and what the site has to connect to. This guide explains the ranges you will see in 2026, what moves a quote up or down, and how to brief a project so the quotes you receive can actually be compared.

## Typical price ranges in 2026

The figures below come from Hostinger India's 2026 website-cost guide. They are market ranges before GST, not ER Freelancer prices. Use them to sense-check quotes, not as fixed packages.

- **Small static site (1–5 pages), freelancer-built:** ₹10,000 – ₹40,000
- **Dynamic business site with a CMS, freelancer-built:** ₹40,000 – ₹1,50,000
- **Small business site, agency-built:** ₹50,000 – ₹1,50,000
- **WooCommerce store, freelancer-built:** ₹25,000 – ₹1,00,000
- **E-commerce site, agency-built:** ₹1,50,000 – ₹4,00,000 and more
- **Custom web application or start-up platform:** ₹2,50,000 – ₹10,00,000 and more

Source: [Hostinger India — How much does a website cost in India in 2026?](https://www.hostinger.com/in/tutorials/website-cost)

## What actually changes the quote

- **Number of unique page templates.** Ten pages built from two templates cost far less than ten pages that are each designed separately.
- **Custom design versus a theme.** A tailored design system takes longer than adapting a well-built theme, but it is easier to extend later.
- **CMS and editing needs.** If your team will update services, prices or blog posts themselves, the content model and editor training are part of the scope.
- **Integrations.** CRM, WhatsApp, payment gateways, booking systems, ERP or accounting software each add design, development and testing time.
- **Content readiness.** Projects move faster and cost less when text, photos and product data are ready before development starts.
- **Speed and SEO baseline.** Mobile performance, structured data and clean URLs should be in the scope from day one, not bolted on after launch.

## Requirements specific to Indian businesses

- **Payments:** customers expect UPI, plus gateways such as Razorpay, PayU, Cashfree, PhonePe PG or Paytm. Gateways usually charge a per-transaction fee, so compare them before you choose.
- **GST invoices:** paid orders need GST-compliant invoices with GSTIN and HSN/SAC codes.
- **E-commerce rules:** online stores must show seller details and a grievance officer under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020.
- **Privacy:** forms that collect personal data should follow the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — clear, purpose-specific consent that users can withdraw. The DPDP Rules, 2025 are being phased in.

This is practical project guidance, not legal advice.

## Running costs people forget

- **Domain:** about ₹500 – ₹1,500 a year for a .com or .in.
- **Hosting:** about ₹2,000 – ₹8,000 a year for standard or managed WordPress hosting; more for cloud or VPS.
- **Maintenance:** updates, backups and small changes — roughly ₹1,500 – ₹10,000 a year for a small site from a freelancer, more for stores and larger sites.
- **Third-party services:** payment gateway fees, email delivery, paid plugins or apps, and any paid fonts or stock images.

The same Hostinger guide is the source for these ranges.

## How to get quotes you can compare

Send every developer the same short brief:

- What the site must achieve (enquiries, bookings, online sales)
- The pages or page types you need, and who will update them
- Systems it must connect to (WhatsApp, CRM, payment gateway, accounting)
- Whether text, photos and product data are ready
- Your launch window and budget range

Then ask each quote to list deliverables, milestones, what is excluded, who owns the code and accounts, and what support costs after launch. A lower number that excludes hosting, content entry or payment testing is not really cheaper.

If you are in Delhi, Noida or Gurugram, the first discovery meeting can be in person on request, with reviews and handover over video calls and a shared staging link. title: Website checklist for businesses in Dubai and the UAE
author: ER Freelancer
excerpt: Arabic and English layouts, UAE data-protection rules, VAT display, local payment methods and the channels UAE customers use — what to plan before you build.
content:
A website that works well in India, the UK or the US often needs real changes before it works for customers in Dubai and the rest of the UAE. Language direction, data-protection rules, payment methods and the channels people use to contact a business are all different. Use this checklist before you brief a designer or developer.

## 1. Arabic and English, done properly

- Decide early whether the site is English-only, Arabic-only or bilingual. Bilingual sites are common for consumer brands, government-facing businesses and real estate.
- Arabic needs a true right-to-left (RTL) layout — navigation, icons, forms and tables all flip. A mirrored English template rarely looks right.
- Give each language its own URL (for example /en/ and /ar/) and add hreflang tags so search engines show the right version.
- Plan Arabic fonts and line spacing separately; Latin font settings make Arabic text cramped.

## 2. Data protection: PDPL, DIFC and ADGM

- Onshore UAE businesses fall under Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection (PDPL).
- Free zones have their own regimes: the DIFC Data Protection Law 2020 and the ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021. Check which one applies to your licence.
- In practice: collect only the data a form needs, explain why, keep a clear privacy notice, and choose hosting and email providers you can document.

Source: [UAE Legislation — Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021](https://uaelegislation.gov.ae/en/legislations/1972). This is practical project guidance, not legal advice.

## 3. Prices, VAT and invoices

- Prices are usually shown VAT-inclusive; the standard UAE VAT rate is 5%.
- Show the currency clearly (AED) and decide whether you also quote USD for international buyers.
- If you sell online, make sure order confirmations and invoices carry the details your accountant needs.

## 4. Payment methods UAE customers expect

- Card and wallet gateways: Network International (N-Genius), Telr, PayTabs, Checkout.com and Stripe, plus Apple Pay.
- Buy-now-pay-later is popular for retail: Tabby and Tamara.
- If you also sell on marketplaces, plan stock and order sync with Amazon.ae or noon from the start.
- Test the full checkout on mobile, including failed payments and refunds.

## 5. Contact channels

- WhatsApp is the first contact channel for many UAE customers — add a WhatsApp button with a pre-filled message, and route enquiries to someone who answers quickly.
- Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok and Snapchat matter depending on the audience; link the ones you actually keep active.
- Show a local phone number (+971) if you have one, and your working hours in UAE time.

## 6. Industry-specific features

- **Real estate:** property listings with filters, maps, floor plans and enquiry forms that reach the right agent.
- **Tourism and hospitality:** direct booking to reduce OTA commission, multilingual tour pages and WhatsApp confirmations.
- **Logistics:** quote requests and shipment tracking.
- **Retail and D2C:** fast mobile storefronts with local payments and BNPL.

## 7. Working across time zones

The UAE is on UTC+4, and India is 1 hour 30 minutes ahead. That leaves about 8.5 hours of overlap in a normal working day, so an Indian development team can join calls in your morning and early afternoon without late nights on either side.

title: Website checklist for UK businesses in 2026
author: ER Freelancer
excerpt: UK GDPR and PECR cookie rules, consumer-contract duties, company details, UK payment methods and how a remote team in India fits your working day.
content:
Building or rebuilding a website for a UK audience? A handful of legal and practical requirements apply whatever your industry. Plan them into the first milestone rather than fixing them after launch.

## 1. Privacy and cookies

- Personal data falls under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. Collect only what each form needs, explain why, and keep a clear privacy notice.
- Cookies and e-marketing are covered by PECR. Most non-essential cookies need prior consent; since February 2026 some analytics and preference cookies are exempt if users get clear information and an easy way to opt out.
- The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 updates parts of both regimes, so check current ICO guidance before you finalise your banner and notices.

Source: [ICO — UK GDPR guidance and resources](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/). This is practical project guidance, not legal advice.

## 2. Company and consumer details

- Limited companies must show their registered name and company number on the website.
- Online shops must follow the Consumer Contracts Regulations, including the 14-day cancellation right for most goods. Put returns, delivery and cancellation information where buyers can find it before they pay.

## 3. Payments UK customers expect

- Card and wallet: Stripe, Worldpay, PayPal and Apple Pay.
- Subscriptions and invoices: GoCardless (Direct Debit) and Open Banking payments.
- Buy-now-pay-later for retail: Klarna.
- If you also sell on Amazon.co.uk, eBay or Etsy, plan stock and order sync from the start.

## 4. Search and contact channels

- Google is the main search engine; write in UK English, use a .co.uk or .uk domain where it helps, and keep service pages specific to the towns you serve.
- LinkedIn matters for B2B, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok for consumer brands; many UK customers also use WhatsApp for quick questions.

## 5. Working hours with a team in India

The UK is on UTC+0 in winter and UTC+1 in summer, so India is 4 h 30 min to 5 h 30 min ahead. That leaves roughly 4.5 hours of overlap in a normal working day. A daily call from 08:00 to 11:00 UK time (13:30–16:30 IST) works all year, and you wake up to the previous day's progress on a staging link.

title: Website checklist for US businesses in 2026
author: ER Freelancer
excerpt: State privacy laws, ADA accessibility, sales tax, US payment methods and how to run a project with a team in India across US time zones.
content:
The US has no single national website rulebook, which is exactly why American projects need a little more planning. Here is what to include in the brief before design starts.

## 1. Privacy: state laws, not one federal law

- There is no single federal privacy law. California's CCPA/CPRA is the best-known state law, and a growing list of other states have their own.
- Sector rules still apply: COPPA covers children's data, CAN-SPAM covers marketing email and the TCPA covers SMS and calls.
- In practice: a clear privacy notice, an opt-out for data sharing where required, and consent records for email and SMS marketing.

Source: [California Privacy Protection Agency — CCPA law and regulations](https://cppa.ca.gov/regulations/). This is practical project guidance, not legal advice.

## 2. Accessibility

ADA lawsuits make WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility a practical requirement for business sites. Build it in from the start: proper headings, labelled forms, keyboard navigation, colour contrast and alt text. Retrofitting later costs more.

## 3. Sales tax and online selling

- Online sellers may owe sales tax in states where they have economic nexus, so choose a store platform and tax tool that can calculate it.
- Plan marketplace sync early if you also sell on Amazon, Walmart Marketplace, Etsy or eBay.

## 4. Payments US customers expect

- Stripe, Square and PayPal for cards, with Apple Pay, Google Pay and Shop Pay for one-tap checkout.
- Buy-now-pay-later: Affirm, Klarna or Afterpay.

## 5. Language and channels

- English first; a Spanish version can widen reach in many states.
- LinkedIn for B2B; Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and YouTube for consumer brands.

## 6. Time zones with a team in India

India is 9 h 30 min to 10 h 30 min ahead of New York and 12 h 30 min to 13 h 30 min ahead of Los Angeles, so working days barely overlap. Projects run on a fixed daily call — for example 08:00–11:00 in New York (18:30–21:30 IST) — with written updates and a staging link in between. Work continues while you sleep, which shortens many timelines.

title: Website checklist for businesses in Saudi Arabia
author: ER Freelancer
excerpt: Arabic-first RTL design, the PDPL, ZATCA e-invoicing and 15% VAT, mada and local payment methods, and the channels Saudi customers use.
content:
Saudi customers expect websites and apps that feel local: Arabic-first, quick on mobile and built around the payment methods and channels they already use. Plan these points before you brief a designer or developer.

## 1. Arabic first, English second

- Arabic-first, right-to-left (RTL) design is expected for consumer brands. Navigation, forms, icons and tables all need a true RTL layout, not a flipped English template.
- Give Arabic and English their own URLs and add hreflang tags so search engines serve the right version.

## 2. Data protection: the PDPL

- The Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) is enforced by SDAIA. Full enforcement began in September 2024.
- Consent and any cross-border transfers need to be documented, so choose hosting and email providers with that in mind.

Source: [SDAIA — Personal Data Protection Law](https://sdaia.gov.sa/en/SDAIA/about/Documents/Personal%20Data%20English%20V2-23April2023-%20Reviewed-.pdf). This is practical project guidance, not legal advice.

## 3. VAT and e-invoicing

- VAT is 15%.
- VAT-registered businesses must issue ZATCA-compliant e-invoices (FATOORA), so an online store or booking system needs an invoicing setup that supports it.

## 4. Payments Saudi customers expect

- mada cards are essential, alongside STC Pay and Apple Pay.
- Gateways: HyperPay, Moyasar and PayTabs.
- Buy-now-pay-later: Tabby and Tamara.
- Marketplaces and store platforms: Amazon.sa, noon, Salla and Zid.

## 5. Channels

Snapchat, X (Twitter), Instagram and TikTok are major channels, and WhatsApp is the usual way to ask a quick question — add a WhatsApp button with a pre-filled message.

## 6. Working hours with a team in India

Saudi Arabia is on UTC+3, and India is 2 h 30 min ahead, leaving about 7.5 hours of overlap in a working day. Calls fit comfortably in your morning and early afternoon.

title: Website checklist for Australian businesses
author: ER Freelancer
excerpt: Privacy Act and Spam Act duties, GST-inclusive pricing, accessibility, Australian payment methods and how a team in India fits your day.
content:
Australian customers expect clear pricing, fast mobile pages and familiar ways to pay. These are the points to cover in your brief before design and development start.

## 1. Privacy and marketing consent

- Personal information is covered by the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles, amended in 2024.
- The Spam Act 2003 requires consent and an unsubscribe option for marketing email and SMS, so forms need clear opt-ins and your email tool needs working unsubscribe links.

Source: [OAIC — The Privacy Act](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-legislation/the-privacy-act). This is practical project guidance, not legal advice.

## 2. Prices and accessibility

- Prices shown to consumers must include GST (10%).
- The Disability Discrimination Act makes WCAG accessibility a practical requirement: readable contrast, labelled forms, keyboard navigation and alt text.

## 3. Payments Australians expect

- Cards and wallets through Stripe, Square or Tyro, plus PayPal.
- Local options: eftpos and PayID / PayTo.
- Buy-now-pay-later: Afterpay and Zip.
- Marketplaces: Amazon.com.au, eBay, Kogan and The Iconic.

## 4. Search and channels

- Use a .com.au or .au domain where it helps, Australian English spelling and service pages for the cities you serve.
- Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn and TikTok are the main social channels.

## 5. Working hours with a team in India

Sydney is 4 h 30 min to 5 h 30 min ahead of India, depending on daylight saving, leaving about 2.5 hours of overlap. A daily call from 13:30 to 16:30 Sydney time (08:00–11:00 IST) works all year, and your afternoon review becomes the team's working day.
